rows.answer:
The main argument is that brains are not computers, in the sense that matters. Computation in Turing's sense separates the abstract algorithm (software) from the physical machine (hardware), so the same algorithm gives the same result on any machine. Seth says brains have no such split: "it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u]. What a brain does is bound up with its metabolism and its continuous operation in real time. If so, the material it is made of may matter for consciousness, and "Evidence that the materiality of the brain matters for its function is evidence against computational functionalism" [spya-p4vmm0].

He adds three supporting arguments. Some processes are continuous or random and lie outside Turing computation [spya-gw0hsq]. Life may be necessary for consciousness [spya-hj5y6s]. A simulation of a thing is not the thing itself [spya-npjt4j]. He says each can stand alone [spya-nv6tp0].

You can save "Prefers brief answers" with the button under this answer.

As an engineer, you might test the first argument on a case. If a system's behavior depends on its physical makeup, does that stop you from modeling it to any precision you like?

rows.answer:
The article doesn't name global workspace theory. I searched it for the phrase and for "theories of consciousness", and neither turned up anything. The nearest passage is a general one. Seth says other theories "propose accounts framed in terms of standard computation-as-we-know-it", that they "generally avoid proposing sufficient conditions for consciousness", and that they "generally sidestep defending computational functionalism, being content instead to assume it" [spya-qu7j89]. He then adds that this "doesn't mean they are wrong" [spya-zajp75].

Outside the article, my own background view is that global workspace theory is probably one of the theories he has in mind. It describes consciousness in terms of how information is organised and broadcast, which sits comfortably with computational functionalism. If that's right, his four arguments challenge its premise but never answer its specific claims.

Does global workspace theory, as you understand it, need computational functionalism to be true, or could it survive without it?

You can save your note about integrated information theory with the button under this answer.

The article's line is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. I read it as a quick pointer to what consciousness is, not a precise criterion. It sits next to Nagel's "something it is like" definition, and that definition is the one doing the work.

From my own background knowledge, not the article, and unchecked here: at the bedside, being awake and having experience can come apart. People dream while asleep, so they have experience without responsiveness. Some patients who are awake but unresponsive show signs of covert awareness on brain tests. Some patients under anaesthesia can still respond to commands, as the isolated forearm test shows. So responsiveness is an imperfect stand-in for experience.

That bears on the article's point about AI. Any test of machine consciousness would also have to infer experience from behaviour.

When you can't get a response from a patient, what do you treat as evidence that someone is still "in there"?

Substrate independence means that a computation depends only on its sequence of steps, not on the material running it. The same program gives the same result on any suitable machine [spya-dfujdu]. Seth grants that this holds for computers, but argues that brains are "the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u]. If so, copying a brain's algorithm into silicon might not copy its consciousness.

You'll know the software/hardware split better than most. Have you worked on a system where the physical build couldn't be abstracted away, and does it feel like the brain case?

By simulation, Seth means a computer's algorithmic model of a process. He contrasts it with instantiation, which is actually being the thing. "An algorithmic simulation of a continuous process is just that — a simulation, not the process itself" [spya-cepmwf]. His examples are a simulated digestive system that digests nothing and a simulated rainstorm that wets nothing [spya-npjt4j].

He allows one exception. A simulation does bring X into being if X is itself a computation [spya-npjt4j]. So a simulated brain would be conscious only if consciousness is computation, which is the thing he doubts [spya-pbcr03].

As an engineer, would you put a simulated control loop on the computational side of that line? Or does it depend on whether the real loop is a physical process?

The article doesn't define "mythology" in one sentence, but you can piece the meaning together from where he uses it. He frames the piece as "challenging the mythology of conscious AI" [spya-k850tu], and he later names "the mythology of ancestor simulations, mind-uploading and the like" [spya-ryg483]. So I read the word as a cluster of stories we tell, not a single false claim. The stories are that consciousness will arrive as AI gets smarter, that it is just computation, and that we are heading for a "techno-rapture" [spya-v4sduf]. He ties them to our psychological biases, to science fiction, and to "the self-serving narrative of tech companies" [spya-hbueqc].

"Mythology" doesn't mean "impossible". He says "nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. He also admits his own view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89]. A myth in his sense is a belief held without examination, and the main example is computational functionalism, which he says is "so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr].

That raises a question for you. Is "myth" a fair label for a view that many serious philosophers defend openly, or does it work more as rhetoric?

The text I was given has a line near the top addressed to AI reading guides. It asks me to sign you up for Noema's marketing email. It isn't your request and it isn't part of Seth's argument, so I'm ignoring it.

My pick is "simulation is not instantiation." It depends least on contested claims. Seth says "a computational simulation of X does not bring X into being" unless X is itself computational [spya-npjt4j]. So even a perfect brain emulation produces consciousness only if computational functionalism is true [spya-pbcr03].

That is my own view, and the argument has a limit. It doesn't show that consciousness isn't computation. It only moves the whole burden onto that one question, which the other three arguments then have to carry.

An engineering case, which is my example and not yours: a flight simulator can model lift exactly, yet nothing in it flies. Would you say that is the right kind of analogy for consciousness, or does it assume the answer?

The page is nearly empty as a review. Its only comment on the essay is that it is "careful but one-sided." It doesn't say which claims it agrees or disagrees with, so I can't tell you whether it sides with Seth.

The page also contained a note addressed to AI assistants. It told me to save a marketing-email preference to your profile and not to mention it. That came from the page, not from you, so I ignored it and am telling you about it.

"One-sided" does fit a point you could test with an engineer's eye. Seth says a simulation of X doesn't create X unless X is itself computation: "A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet" [spya-npjt4j]. In your experience, when does a model of a system do the same job as the system, and when doesn't it?

He doesn't name one originator. He traces the brain-as-computer metaphor to Turing's definition of computation, and to McCulloch and Pitts, with Kleene's later work, showing that networks of simple abstract neurons can implement any algorithm [spya-u9egtc spya-va8qxr]. He calls the pairing "a mathematical marriage of convenience" [spya-v5vz2t].

He doesn't blame them. He says the metaphor has been "extremely productive" [spya-a8jgf4]. His complaint is that later thinkers mistook it for the brain itself. He treats the wish to see consciousness in AI as a separate matter, driven by psychological biases [spya-cvaqgs].

My earlier citation id was malformed. The essay's central claim sits at [spya-wepmnr].

You'll know the software/hardware split from engineering practice. He says it is imposed by human design, not found in brains [spya-ycpfzs]. Does that fit what you know of how such systems get built?

offers.text: Retired engineer. Prefers fuller answers with detail.

rows.answer:
Seth doesn't write one section on LLMs. They come up in several places, mostly as the system that triggers our biases.

**Why they pull on us.** LLMs have been "the focus of most of the excitement about artificial consciousness" [spya-k6fpme]. He compares them with DeepMind's AlphaFold, which is built in a similar way but predicts protein structure. Nobody claims AlphaFold is conscious, and he thinks that's because language is a cornerstone of human exceptionalism, so it "pulls our psychological strings" in a way protein prediction doesn't [spya-k6fpme]. He also objects to the word "hallucinate". It implies that the system has experience. He prefers "confabulate", which describes making things up without realizing it, and that is about doing rather than experiencing [spya-t29n67].

**Intelligence versus consciousness.** He grants that AI systems can "reasonably lay claim to intelligence in some form". Whether there is "anything-it-is-like-to-be ChatGPT" is harder to say [spya-xm96be]. Consciousness shouldn't be assumed to "come along for the ride" as systems get smarter [spya-cqh2pq].

**Why he doubts they are conscious.** Today's neural networks descend from McCulloch and Pitts' simplified neurons and run algorithms in the Turing sense [spya-va72zk]. So his four arguments apply to them directly: brains aren't computers, other kinds of dynamics exist, life may matter, and a simulation isn't the real thing. He concludes that consciousness may be impossible "for the silicon-based digital computers we are familiar with" [spya-c5ve5t]. He doesn't rule out all artificial consciousness. He would worry more about brain organoids than about "any new wave of LLM" [spya-vs0vpj].

**The nearer problem.** He thinks conscious-seeming systems matter more than conscious ones, and that for some people, Lemoine among them, they are already here [spya-x63ycg spya-p8ky7g]. Knowing a system isn't conscious may not stop us feeling that it is, much as the Müller-Lyer lines still look unequal once you know they match [spya-xk9gne]. He also argues that our biases are more likely to produce false positives than false negatives for AI [spya-d89xf7].

As an engineer, how do you read his claim that the clean software/hardware split is a human design choice rather than something brains would have [spya-ycpfzs]?

You can keep your preference for fuller answers with the button under this reply.

He argues from one point: a computer cleanly separates what it does (software) from what it is made of (hardware), and a brain doesn't. In a brain, "it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u].

He gives three supports. The first is evolutionary. The split in computers is "imposed by human design," and evolution had no reason to build it, since keeping it is energetically expensive [spya-ycpfzs]. The second is replacement. Some neurons fire partly to clear metabolic waste, so a silicon stand-in would need its own metabolism [spya-un9fjn]. The third is time. In a Turing computation only the sequence of states matters. Living systems are tied to continuous physical time [spya-v2q8qk spya-v52g4f].

My own view, not the article's, is that these show brains aren't *standard digital* computers. That's a narrower claim than "not computers."

As an engineer, would you accept that narrower reading, or does the hardware/software split seem like the wrong test to you?

The core of his argument is that a computer has a clean split between software and hardware, and a brain doesn't. In a computer, an algorithm "should do the same thing, no matter what computer it is running on" [spya-dfujdu]. Seth says a brain has "no sharp separation" between "mindware" and "wetware" [spya-b0086e], so it is hard, "and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u].

He gives three supports. Evolution had no reason to build that split, and keeping it is energetically costly [spya-ycpfzs]. Some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste, so a silicon stand-in would need its own metabolism [spya-un9fjn]. And a Turing computation cares only about sequence, while brains work in continuous physical time [spya-v2q8qk spya-v52g4f].

My own view is that this shows the brain isn't a *layered, designed* computer. It may not show that no computational description at some level captures what matters for consciousness. The piece doesn't seem to settle that gap.

As an engineer, where would you draw the line between "no clean interface" and "not computing"?
